cards.q: 168 people were surveyed: 64 own a cat and a dog, 48 own a dog only and 19 own neither. How many own a cat only?
cards.why: All four regions of the Venn diagram add to 168, so cats only = 168 − 19 − 64 − 48 = 37. The 19 go outside both circles.
cards.hook: Venn regions add up to the total: take away the ones you know.

cards.q: 168 people surveyed: 37 own a cat only, 64 a cat and a dog, 48 a dog only, 19 neither. One is picked at random. What is the probability they own both a cat and a dog?
cards.why: Both = the overlap, 64 people. Divide by everyone surveyed, 168 (the 19 with no pet were surveyed too): 64/168 = 8/21.
cards.hook: Probability = how many fit ÷ everyone who could be picked.

cards.q: 168 surveyed: 37 own a cat only, 64 a cat and a dog, 48 a dog only, 19 neither. What percentage own one animal only, correct to one decimal place?
cards.why: One animal only = cats only + dogs only = 37 + 48 = 85 (leave out the 64 with both). 85 ÷ 168 × 100 = 50.59…% ≈ 50.6%.
cards.hook: "Only one" leaves out the overlap. A percentage: × 100.

cards.q: In a Venn diagram of cat owners and dog owners, which regions hold the people who own one animal only?
wrong: Cats only, dogs only and both
The overlap of the two circles
cards.why: One animal only means a cat but no dog, or a dog but no cat: the two parts of the circles that don't overlap. The overlap owns two; outside owns none.
cards.hook: Only one = the circles without the overlap.
keys: the two parts of the circles that don't overlap

cards.q: Mandy picks Balcony or Stalls, then Monday, Wednesday or Friday, then VIP or show only. All choices are equally likely. What is the probability that she chooses a VIP ticket on a Wednesday?
cards.why: Two paths fit: B→W→V and S→W→V, each ½ × ⅓ × ½ = 1/12. Add them: 1/12 + 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6. Or: 2 of the 12 equally likely outcomes.
cards.hook: Multiply along a path; add the paths that fit.

cards.q: Mandy chooses Balcony or Stalls, then Monday, Wednesday or Friday, then VIP or show only. How many outcomes does the finished tree diagram have?
cards.why: Each seat splits into 3 days, and each day into 2 ticket types: 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 outcomes at the ends of the branches. 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 adds instead.
cards.hook: Tree outcomes = the numbers of branches multiplied.

cards.q: 65 909 babies were born in Ireland in 2015, and 32 290 of them were girls. How many boys were born?
cards.why: Every baby is a boy or a girl, so boys = all babies − girls = 65 909 − 32 290 = 33 619. Check by adding back: 33 619 + 32 290 = 65 909.
cards.hook: Check a subtraction by adding the answer back.

cards.q: Of the 65 909 babies born in 2015, 33 619 were boys. What is the probability that a baby picked at random is a boy, correct to 2 decimal places?
cards.why: P(boy) = boys ÷ all babies = 33 619 ÷ 65 909 = 0.5100… ≈ 0.51. Divide by all the babies, not by the girls, and use the real counts, not 50:50.
cards.hook: Probability = what you want ÷ the total.

cards.q: P(a baby is a boy) = 0.51, and births are independent. 8 babies are born in a hospital one day. What is the probability that the first three are boys, to 4 decimal places?
cards.why: Independent births: multiply. 0.51 × 0.51 × 0.51 = 0.132651 ≈ 0.1327. The other 5 babies can be boys or girls, so they don't come into it.
cards.hook: Independent events one after another: multiply.

cards.q: P(a baby is a boy) = 0.51, and births are independent. What is the probability that the third birth was the first girl born that day, to 4 decimal places?
cards.why: Third birth the first girl: boy, boy, girl. P(girl) = 1 − 0.51 = 0.49, so 0.51 × 0.51 × 0.49 = 0.127449 ≈ 0.1274. One order only: no × 3.
cards.hook: "First … on the 3rd": fail, fail, then succeed.

cards.q: "The third baby born was the first girl born that day." Which outcomes for births 1, 2 and 3 does this mean?
wrong: Any order with exactly one girl
Boy, boy, then a boy or a girl
cards.why: The first girl comes 3rd, so births 1 and 2 must both be boys, and birth 3 a girl. Only that one order fits.
cards.hook: First success on go 3 = fail, fail, success.
keys: births 1 and 2 must both be boys

cards.q: Probability of being born on each day: Mon 0.14, Tue ?, Wed 0.15, Thu 0.18, Fri 0.15, Sat 0.12, Sun 0.1. What is the probability for Tuesday?
cards.why: The six known ones add to 0.14 + 0.15 + 0.18 + 0.15 + 0.12 + 0.1 = 0.84. All seven add to 1, so Tuesday = 1 − 0.84 = 0.16. (Sunday 0.1 = 0.10.)
cards.hook: The probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1.

cards.q: Why must the probabilities of being born on Monday, Tuesday, …, Sunday add up to exactly 1?
cards.right: Every baby is born on exactly one day
wrong: There are 7 days in the week
cards.why: The seven days cover every possible outcome, and no baby is born on two days, so together they are certain: total probability 1.
cards.hook: Outcomes that cover everything, with no overlap, add to 1.

cards.q: P(a baby is born on a Tuesday) = 0.16. In one week 1300 babies were born. How many babies would you expect to be born on the Tuesday of that week?
cards.why: Expected number = total × probability = 1300 × 0.16 = 208. (1300 ÷ 7 would treat all days as equally likely, but Tuesday's is 0.16.)
cards.hook: Expected number = how many there are × the probability.

cards.q: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores added. A table shows the total for every pair of scores (Die 1 across, Die 2 down). How many cells does it have?
cards.why: Each of Die 1's 6 scores goes with each of Die 2's 6 scores: 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes. 11 is only the number of different totals (2 to 12).
cards.hook: Count outcomes, not totals: two dice give 6 × 6 = 36.

cards.q: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores added. What is the probability of getting a total of 7 or 11?
cards.why: Six of the 36 outcomes make 7 (1+6, 2+5, … 6+1) and two make 11 (5+6, 6+5). A total can't be both, so add: 8/36 = 2/9.
cards.hook: "Or" with no overlap: add the counts.

cards.q: Two dice: P(total of 7 or 11) = 6/36 + 2/36. Why can you simply add the two here?
cards.right: A total can't be 7 and 11 at once
cards.why: No outcome is in both groups (they are mutually exclusive), so nothing is counted twice and P(7 or 11) = P(7) + P(11).
cards.hook: Add for "or" only when nothing can be in both.

cards.q: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores added. What is the probability that the total is a prime number?
cards.why: Prime totals: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. They come up 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15 times in the 36 outcomes: 15/36 = 5/12. (9 = 3 × 3 is not prime.)
cards.hook: Primes up to 12: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11. Then count outcomes.

cards.q: Two dice are thrown and the scores added. Which of the possible totals are prime numbers?
cards.why: A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. 2 is prime (the only even one); 9 = 3 × 3 is not. The totals run 2 to 12, so: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.
cards.hook: 2 is prime; 9 isn't (3 × 3).

cards.q: 30 cars: 18 Fords (7 of them red) and 12 Renaults (4 of them red). One car is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is a Ford or a car which is not red?
cards.why: All 18 Fords, plus the Renaults that are not red: 12 − 4 = 8. Not-red Fords are already in the 18. 18 + 8 = 26, so 26/30 = 13/15. (Or 30 − 4.)
cards.hook: "Or": count everything in either group, but each car only once.

cards.q: 30 cars: Ford 18 (7 red, 11 not red), Renault 12 (4 red, 8 not red). Which cars are NOT "a Ford or not red"?
cards.why: A car fails "Ford or not red" only if it is not a Ford and is red: a red Renault. There are 4, so P = (30 − 4)/30 = 26/30.
cards.hook: Tricky "or"? Count what fits neither, and take it away.

cards.q: Find the number of different arrangements that can be made using all the letters of the word RAINBOW, each letter used only once.
cards.why: 7 different letters fill 7 places: 7, then 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 options. 7! = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 5040.
cards.hook: All n different letters in a row: n! (the x! key).

cards.q: Arranging all 7 letters of RAINBOW: why is it 7 × 6 × 5 × … and not 7 × 7 × 7 × …?
cards.right: Each letter is used only once
wrong: There are 7 letters to choose from
The order of the letters matters
cards.why: Once a letter is placed it can't be used again, so each place has one option fewer: 7, 6, 5, … 7 × 7 × 7 × … would let letters repeat.
cards.hook: No repeats: the options drop by 1 at each place.
keys: each place has one option fewer

cards.q: How many different 3-letter arrangements can be made using the letters of the word RAINBOW, each letter used at most once?
cards.why: 3 places, 7 letters, no repeats: 7 × 6 × 5 = 210. Order matters (RAI isn't IAR), so not ⁷C₃ = 35; no repeats, so not 7³ = 343.
cards.hook: Stop after 3 places: 7 × 6 × 5, not 7!.

cards.q: A spinner has 7 sectors: red 72°, orange 30°, yellow 45°, green 90°, blue 60°, indigo 18°, violet 45°. Yellow's probability is 1/8. What is the probability of red?
cards.why: Probability = the sector's angle ÷ 360° (check: yellow 45/360 = 1/8). Red: 72/360 = 1/5. The sectors aren't equal, so not 1/7.
cards.hook: Spinner probability = angle ÷ 360°.

cards.q: A spinner has 7 sectors of different sizes. How do you find the probability of it stopping in each sector?
cards.why: A sector's chance is the fraction of the full turn it covers: its angle ÷ 360°. 1/7 only works if all 7 sectors are the same size.
cards.hook: Fraction of the circle = fraction of the time.
keys: the fraction of the full turn it covers

cards.q: Spinner prizes (probability): red €20 (1/5), orange €60 (1/12), yellow €24 (1/8), green €8 (1/4), blue €42 (1/6), indigo €90 (1/20), violet €48 (1/8). Expected prize?
cards.why: E(X) = Σ prize × probability = 4 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 7 + 4.5 + 6 = €31.50. Add all seven products, and don't divide by 7.
cards.hook: Expected value: each value × its probability, then add them all.

cards.q: A spinner game has seven prizes, each with its own probability. How do you find the expected value of the prize?
cards.right: Add up prize × probability for all 7
wrong: Add the 7 prizes and divide by 7
The prize of the likeliest colour
cards.why: E(X) = Σ x·P(x): multiply each prize by its probability and add all seven. Dividing by 7 would treat every colour as equally likely.
cards.hook: E(X) = Σ x × P(x).

cards.q: In a population, the probability that a person has blue eyes is 0.7. One person is chosen at random. What is the probability that they do not have blue eyes?
cards.why: A person either has blue eyes or doesn't, so the two add to 1: P(not blue) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. A probability is never more than 1 (30% = 0.3).
cards.hook: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

cards.q: P(a person has blue eyes) = 0.7. Two people are chosen at random. What is the probability that both have blue eyes?
cards.why: The two people are independent, so multiply along blue, blue: 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49. (0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09 is the chance that neither has blue eyes.)
cards.hook: "Both", with independent people: multiply.

cards.q: P(blue eyes) = 0.7. Why can you multiply 0.7 × 0.7 for two people chosen at random from a large population?
cards.right: One person's eyes don't affect another's
wrong: Both people have the same probability
cards.why: Multiplying works for independent events: one person's eye colour doesn't change the chance for the next, so P(blue, blue) = 0.7 × 0.7.
cards.hook: Multiply only when one result doesn't change the other's chance.

cards.q: P(a person has blue eyes) = 0.7. Three people are chosen at random. What is the probability that exactly two of them have blue eyes?
cards.why: One order: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.147. The person without blue eyes can be 1st, 2nd or 3rd, so × 3: 3 × 0.147 = 0.441.
cards.hook: Exactly 2 of 3: one order's chance × 3.

cards.q: Three people are chosen. Which list shows every way that exactly two have blue eyes (B = blue, N = not blue)?
cards.why: Exactly two blue means exactly one N, and the N can be in any of the 3 places: BBN, BNB, NBB. BBB has three blue, so it doesn't count.
cards.hook: Exactly 2: list every place the odd one out can go.

cards.q: P(a person has blue eyes) = 0.7. Four people are chosen one after another. What is the probability that the fourth person is the only one with blue eyes?
cards.why: Not, not, not, blue: 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.0189. The question names the 4th person, so only this one order counts: no × 4.
cards.hook: Named position? One order only.

cards.q: Twister: one spinner gives Left Hand, Right Hand, Left Foot or Right Foot; the other gives Yellow, Red, Blue or Green. How many different outcomes are there?
cards.why: Each of the 4 body parts can go with each of the 4 colours: 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes (a 4 by 4 table). 4 + 4 = 8 counts the sections, not the pairs.
cards.hook: Two spinners: multiply their numbers of sections.

cards.q: Twister: spinner 1 gives LH, RH, LF or RF; spinner 2 gives one of 4 colours (equal sections). Kate spins both once. What is the probability that she must use her left foot?
cards.why: Left foot is a whole row of the 4 × 4 table: 4 of the 16 outcomes, any colour. 4/16 = 1/4 (or just spinner 1: 1 of its 4 sections).
cards.hook: Only one spinner matters? Use just that spinner.

cards.q: Twister: the colour spinner has 4 equal sections: Yellow, Red, Blue and Green. Kate spins both spinners once. What is the probability of a red or yellow spot?
cards.why: Red and Yellow are 2 of the 4 colours: 8 of the 16 outcomes, or 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. A spot can't be both, so just add. Multiplying is for "and".
cards.hook: "Or" with no overlap: add.

cards.q: Twister: spinner 1 has 4 equal sections (LH, RH, LF, RF), spinner 2 has 4 equal colours. Jack spins both. What is the probability of his right hand and a blue spot?
cards.why: Right hand and blue is one cell of the 16-cell table: 1/16. Or, as the spinners are independent, 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Adding 1/4 + 1/4 is for "or".
cards.hook: "And" with independent spinners: multiply.

cards.q: Twister: spinner 1 has 4 equal sections (LH, RH, LF, RF), spinner 2 has 4 equal colours. Jack spins both. What is the probability of his right hand or a blue spot?
cards.why: Right hand is a row of 4, blue a column of 4, and they share 1 cell. 4/16 + 4/16 − 1/16 = 7/16: take off the shared cell so it's counted once.
cards.hook: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

cards.q: Twister: P(right hand or blue) = 4/16 + 4/16 − 1/16. Why take away the 1/16?
cards.right: Right hand AND blue was counted twice
wrong: Right hand with blue doesn't count
Blue is only one of the 4 colours
cards.why: Right hand + blue is in the right-hand row AND the blue column, so 4 + 4 counts it twice. Take 1 off so it is counted once: it still counts.
cards.hook: "Or" means either one or both: count the overlap once.

cards.q: At a fun fair stall, the probability of knocking a coconut off its support is 0.34. What is the probability of not knocking it off?
cards.why: You either knock it off or you don't, so the two add to 1: P(not) = 1 − 0.34 = 0.66. Keep it a decimal: 66 is the percentage (66%).
cards.hook: P(not) = 1 − P(it happens).

cards.q: P(knocking the coconut off) = 0.34 each go, independently. David has three goes. What is the probability he knocks it off for the first time on his third go, to 3 d.p.?
cards.why: First time on the 3rd go: miss, miss, hit. 0.66 × 0.66 × 0.34 = 0.148104 ≈ 0.148. One order only, so no × 3.
cards.hook: First success on go 3: miss, miss, hit.

cards.q: Figure ABCDE: a large square ACDE stands on the diagonal [AC] of a small square ABCF with side 2 cm, so triangle ABC sticks out below it. Find the area of ABCDE.
cards.why: |AC|² = 2² + 2² = 8, so the big square is √8 × √8 = 8 cm². Triangle ABC is half the small square: ½ × 2 × 2 = 2. Total 8 + 2 = 10 cm².
cards.hook: Square on a diagonal: Pythagoras gives its side; side² its area.

cards.q: Figure ABCDE: a large square ACDE on the diagonal [AC] of a small square ABCF (side 2 cm), where |AC| = √8 cm. Find the perimeter of ABCDE, to two decimal places.
cards.why: Go round the outside: AB + BC + CD + DE + EA = 2 + 2 + √8 + √8 + √8 = 4 + 3√8 = 12.485… ≈ 12.49 cm. AC is inside, so leave it out.
cards.hook: Perimeter: only the outside edges. Lines inside don't count.

cards.q: Rohan scores 70% of his free throws, and his throws are independent. What is the probability that he scores his first 3 free throws?
cards.why: P(score) = 0.7 each time, and the throws are independent, so multiply: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.343. (0.027 is missing all three.)
cards.hook: Independent, and all three must happen: multiply three times.

cards.q: Rohan scores 70% of his free throws, independently. What is the probability that he scores exactly 2 of his first 3 free throws?
cards.why: A miss is 1 − 0.7 = 0.3. One order: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.147. The miss can be 1st, 2nd or 3rd (SSF, SFS, FSS), so 3 × 0.147 = 0.441.
cards.hook: Exactly 2 of 3: one order's chance × 3.

cards.q: Rohan scores each free throw with probability 0.7. Why is 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.147 not the answer to "exactly 2 of his first 3"?
cards.right: It is only one order: score, score, miss
wrong: It leaves out 0.343 for all three
They should be added, not multiplied
cards.why: 0.147 is the chance of S, S, F in that order. SFS and FSS also give exactly 2 scores, each 0.147, so the answer is 3 × 0.147 = 0.441.
cards.hook: Same chance for each order? Multiply by how many orders.
keys: SFS and FSS also give exactly 2 scores

cards.q: Give one reason why Rohan scoring his free throws might not be independent events.
cards.right: A miss may make him nervous next time
wrong: Every throw has the same 0.7 chance
Each throw is either a score or a miss
cards.why: Independent means one throw doesn't change the chance of the next. But earlier throws can affect him: a miss may make him nervous, a score more confident.
cards.hook: Not independent = one result changes the next one's chance.
keys: one throw doesn't change the chance of the next

cards.q: Points Rohan scored (number of games): 0 (4 games), 6 (5), 8 (4), 10 (2), 12 (3), 16 (1). Find his mean number of points per game, to 2 decimal places.
cards.hook: Mean from a frequency table: Σfx ÷ Σf.

cards.q: Rohan's frequency table gives a total of 134 points over all his games. To find his mean points per game, what do you divide 134 by?
wrong: 52, the total of the point values
cards.why: The mean is per game, so divide by the number of games: 4 + 5 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 19, including the 4 games where he scored 0.
cards.hook: Divide by Σf (how many games), not by the number of columns.
keys: divide by the number of games

cards.q: A regular pentagon ABCDE is split into five congruent isosceles triangles meeting at its centre O, and |∠BOC| = 72°. Find |∠CBA|.
cards.why: |OB| = |OC|, so triangle BOC's base angles are (180° − 72°) ÷ 2 = 54°. ∠CBA is two of them, ∠OBC + ∠OBA: 54° + 54° = 108°.
cards.hook: Isosceles: the two base angles are equal; share what's left of 180°.

cards.q: Triangle AOB in a regular pentagon has |OA| = |OB| = 6 cm and |∠AOB| = 72°. Find its area, correct to 1 decimal place.
cards.why: Two sides and the angle between them: Area = ½ab sin C = ½(6)(6) sin 72° = 17.119… ≈ 17.1 cm². Calculator in degrees (radians gives 4.6).
cards.hook: Two sides and the angle between: Area = ½ab sin C.

cards.q: A regular pentagon is made of 5 congruent triangles, each with sides 6 cm and 6 cm and 72° between them (area 17.119… cm²). Find the pentagon's area, to 1 decimal place.
cards.why: The pentagon is 5 of the triangles: 17.119… × 5 = 85.59… ≈ 85.6 cm². Use the unrounded value: 17.1 × 5 = 85.5 has lost accuracy.
cards.hook: Round only at the very end.

cards.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 5 is spun twice, and each number landed on is recorded. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
cards.why: Each of the 5 first spins goes with each of the 5 second spins: 5 × 5 = 25 pairs, (1,1) to (5,5). (1,2) and (2,1) are different outcomes.
cards.hook: Two-way table: rows × columns.

cards.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 5 is spun twice and the two numbers are added. What are the maximum and minimum possible totals?
cards.why: The same number can come up on both spins. Biggest: 5 + 5 = 10. Smallest: 1 + 1 = 2.
cards.hook: Spun twice: the same number can come up both times.

cards.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 5 (each equally likely) is spun twice and the two numbers are added. What is the probability of a total of either 4 or 5?
cards.hook: Count outcomes in the 25-cell table, not totals.

cards.q: Jena pays €1 to spin. N: probability 0.3, she gets €1. S: 0.2, €0.50. E: 0.4, €0. W: 0.1, €5. What is the expected value of the money she gets?
cards.hook: Each amount × its probability, then add all four.

cards.q: Jena pays €1 for each spin, and the expected value of the money she gets back is €0.90. Is the game fair?
cards.right: No: on average she loses 10c a go
wrong: Yes: the probabilities add up to 1
No: she gets nothing 40% of the time
cards.why: A fair game gives back, on average, what you pay. She pays €1 and expects €0.90 back: €0.90 < €1, so she loses 10c a go. Not fair.
cards.hook: Fair: the expected payout equals the cost to play.

cards.q: Seán's cards: green ones numbered 1 to 7 and red ones numbered 1 to 7. A table has Colour (G, R) down the side and Number (1 to 7) across. How many outcomes does it show?
cards.why: Each of the 2 colours goes with each of the 7 numbers: 2 × 7 = 14 cells, G1 to G7 and R1 to R7: one for each card.
cards.hook: Outcomes in a table = rows × columns.

cards.q: Seán has 14 cards: green G1 to G7 and red R1 to R7. A card is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has an even number?
cards.why: Even numbers are 2, 4 and 6 in both colours: G2, G4, G6, R2, R4, R6. That's 6 of the 14 cards: 6/14 = 3/7. (1 to 7 has more odds than evens.)
cards.hook: List the cards that fit, in every colour.

cards.q: Seán's 14 cards: G1–G7 and R1–R7. He picks a card, Red 5, and doesn't put it back. He then picks a second card at random. What is the probability that it is green?
cards.why: R5 is not put back, so 13 cards are left. It wasn't green, so all 7 greens are still there: P(green) = 7/13.
cards.hook: Without replacement: the total goes down by one.

cards.q: Seán's 14 cards: G1–G7 and R1–R7. He picks a card, doesn't replace it, then picks a second. What is the probability the 2nd is a different colour and a different number?
cards.why: Say the first is G3: 13 cards are left. A different colour means a red card (7), and a different number rules out R3: 7 − 1 = 6. So 6/13.
cards.hook: Without replacement, two conditions: count the cards left that fit both.

cards.q: Hours of sleep are normally distributed, and the middle 68% slept between 7.2 and 8.4 hours. Which values go in the axis boxes: left of 7.2, in the middle, right of 8.4?
cards.why: 68% is μ ± σ, so μ = (7.2 + 8.4) ÷ 2 = 7.8 and 2σ = 8.4 − 7.2 = 1.2, so σ = 0.6. The outer boxes are μ ± 2σ: 6.6 and 9.0.
cards.hook: Empirical rule: 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ.

cards.q: On a normal curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the middle 68% of the data lies between which two values?
cards.why: The empirical rule: about 68% lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean (μ ± σ), 95% within 2 (μ ± 2σ) and 99.7% within 3 (μ ± 3σ).
keys: within 1 standard deviation of the mean

cards.q: Sleep is normally distributed with mean 7.8 hours and standard deviation 0.6 hours. Using the empirical rule, what percentage got at least 9 hours of sleep?
cards.why: 9 = 7.8 + 2(0.6) = μ + 2σ. 95% lie between 6.6 and 9.0; the other 5% splits equally between the two ends, so 2.5% got 9 hours or more.
cards.hook: Only one end? Halve what's outside.

cards.q: Owen gets the recommended amount of sleep 10% of the time. What is the probability that he does not get the recommended amount of sleep on a particular night?
cards.why: 10% = 0.1 is the chance he does get enough sleep. Enough or not enough: they add to 1, so P(not) = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9 (that is 90%).
cards.hook: Change % to a decimal first, then use 1 − P.

cards.q: Owen gets enough sleep on a night with probability 0.1, independently each night. Starting Sunday, what is the probability that Tuesday (the 3rd night) is the first night with enough sleep?
cards.why: First time on Tuesday: Sunday no, Monday no, Tuesday yes. The nights are independent, so multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.081.
cards.hook: First success on the 3rd try: fail × fail × success.

cards.q: An ice cream van sells 7 flavours, 4 toppings, and a cone or a tub. How many different choices are there of one flavour, one topping, and a cone or a tub?
cards.why: One from each group: 7 × 4 × 2 = 56. Every flavour goes with every topping, and each pair comes in a cone or a tub. 7 + 4 + 2 = 13 counts items.
cards.hook: Choices from separate groups: multiply.

cards.q: 7 flavours, 4 toppings, 2 containers: 56 choices. How many choices would there be with one extra flavour, and how many with one extra topping instead?
cards.why: Extra flavour: 8 × 4 × 2 = 64. Extra topping: 7 × 5 × 2 = 70. 70 > 64, so he should add a topping.
cards.hook: An extra topping pairs with 7 × 2 = 14 others; a flavour only with 4 × 2 = 8.

cards.q: 100 customers: 42 bought vanilla (V), 37 bought a cone (C), and 45 bought neither vanilla nor a cone. How many bought vanilla in a cone (both)?
cards.why: 100 − 45 = 55 are inside the circles. 42 + 37 = 79 counts the overlap twice, so 79 − 55 = 24 bought both. Then V only 18 and C only 13.
cards.hook: Both circles added − people inside = the overlap.

cards.q: 100 customers: 42 bought vanilla, 37 a cone, 45 neither. Why is 42 + 37 = 79 more than the 55 people inside the two circles?
cards.right: Those who bought both were counted twice
wrong: The 45 outside were counted as well
Some customers bought two ice creams
cards.why: Anyone with vanilla in a cone is in the 42 and in the 37, so adding counts those people twice. The extra, 79 − 55 = 24, is the overlap.
cards.hook: Adding two circles counts the overlap twice.

cards.q: Venn diagram of 100 customers: vanilla only 18, vanilla and cone 24, cone only 13, neither 45. What is P(a customer bought a cone with a flavour other than vanilla)?
cards.why: A cone but not vanilla is the cone-only region: 13 of the 100 customers, so 13/100 = 0.13. The 24 in the overlap had vanilla.
cards.hook: "A but not B" = the part of A's circle outside B.

cards.q: Typical Sunday sales: wet €150 (probability 30%), dry and cold €200 (45%), dry and warm €450 (25%). What is the expected value of next Sunday's sales?
cards.hook: Percentages → decimals before you multiply.

cards.q: A cone logo: a sector of radius 20 cm, angle θ at the centre, sits on two right-angled triangles whose angles at the centre are 70° each. Find θ.
cards.why: The angles all the way round the centre add to 360°. The two 70° angles belong to the triangles, so θ = 360° − 2(70°) = 220°.
cards.hook: Angles round a point add up to 360°.

cards.q: A sector has radius 20 cm and angle 220° at the centre. Find the length of its arc s, correct to 1 decimal place.
cards.why: Arc = (θ/360) × 2πr = (220/360) × 2π(20) = 76.79… ≈ 76.8 cm. (θ/360) × πr² would be the sector's area, not its arc.
cards.hook: Arc: (θ/360) × 2πr. Area: (θ/360) × πr².

cards.q: In the logo, a right-angled triangle has a 70° angle at the centre, the 20 cm radius next to that angle (adjacent) and side l opposite it. Find l, to the nearest cm.
cards.why: Opposite and adjacent: use tan. tan 70° = l/20, so l = 20 tan 70° = 54.9… ≈ 55 cm (calculator in degrees).
cards.hook: SOH CAH TOA: opposite and adjacent → tan.

cards.q: A right-angled triangle has a 70° angle. The side next to it (adjacent) is 20 cm, and side l is opposite it. Which equation gives l?
cards.why: tan = opposite ÷ adjacent. l is opposite the 70° and 20 is adjacent, so tan 70° = l/20. (cos 70° = 20/l would find the hypotenuse.)
cards.hook: TOA: Tan = Opposite ÷ Adjacent.

cards.q: Seán wins match 1 with probability 0.6 and match 2 with probability 0.7, independently. On a tree diagram, what goes on the "Win match 2" branch after he loses match 1?
cards.why: The matches are independent, so match 2's chances don't depend on match 1: Win 0.7 (and Lose 0.3), after a win or after a loss.
cards.hook: Independent: the second set of branches is the same every time.
keys: match 2's chances don't depend on match 1

cards.q: Tree: match 1 Win 0.6, Lose 0.4; match 2 Win 0.7, Lose 0.3 (independent). Win-Win = 0.42 and Lose-Lose = 0.12. What are Win-Lose and Lose-Win?
cards.hook: Along a path: multiply. The ends of the tree add up to 1.

cards.q: Two matches: P(Win-Win) = 0.42, P(Win-Lose) = 0.18, P(Lose-Win) = 0.28, P(Lose-Lose) = 0.12. What is the probability that Seán wins at least 1 match?
cards.why: At least 1 win is every outcome except Lose-Lose: 1 − 0.12 = 0.88. (Or 0.42 + 0.18 + 0.28 = 0.88: Win-Win counts too.)
cards.hook: At least one = 1 − none.

cards.q: Seán plays two matches and wins or loses each. What is the quickest way to find the probability that he wins at least 1 match?
cards.why: "At least 1 win" leaves out only Lose-Lose, so take that from 1. P(W-L) + P(L-W) is exactly one win; 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3 is more than 1.
cards.hook: At least one? 1 − P(none).

cards.q: Each time Sarah plays a service game, the probability that she wins it is 0.78. What is the probability that she loses her next service game?
cards.why: Each game she either wins or loses, so P(lose) = 1 − P(win) = 1 − 0.78 = 0.22.
cards.hook: Win or lose, nothing else: P(lose) = 1 − P(win).

cards.q: Sarah wins each service game with probability 0.78, independently. What is the probability that the first service game she loses is her third, to 3 decimal places?
cards.why: First loss on game 3: win, win, lose. 0.78 × 0.78 × 0.22 = 0.133848 ≈ 0.134. One order only: no × 3.
cards.hook: First loss on game 3: win, win, lose.

cards.q: A child's football is a sphere with a diameter of 18 cm. Find its volume, in cm³, in terms of π.
cards.why: r = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm. V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π(9)³ = (4/3) × 729π = 972π cm³. Leave π as a letter.
cards.hook: Given the diameter? Halve it first.

cards.q: An adult's football is a sphere with a volume of 5424.6 cm³. Work out its radius, correct to 1 decimal place.
cards.hook: Undo r³ with a cube root (∛).

cards.q: A team had 15 shots: 6 with a 10% chance of a goal, 5 with 20%, 3 with 40% and 1 with 70%. What are the Expected Goals (the expected number of goals)?
cards.why: Each shot is worth its probability in goals: 6(0.1) + 5(0.2) + 3(0.4) + 1(0.7) = 0.6 + 1 + 1.2 + 0.7 = 3.5 goals.
cards.hook: Expected number = Σ (how many × probability).
